title: Clinical Decision-Making in Neurogenetics
description: A decision-making framework that follows the patient journey — choosing the first test, reading an ambiguous report, acting on a result, managing the diagnosis, and counseling the family — connecting genetic findings to real clinical care.
learningObjectives: Select panel vs. exome vs. genome (and trio vs. singleton) from phenotype, inheritance pattern, and turnaround needs
Counsel a family about a VUS — what it does and does not mean, and when re-contact is warranted
Recognize when a negative genetic result is not a true negative and choose the right next step
Distinguish symptomatic from disease-modifying treatment and locate guideline-based surveillance schedules
Map the reproductive decision points: prenatal diagnosis, PGT-M, cascade testing, and donor options
Communicate prognosis honestly under genotype–phenotype uncertainty and coordinate multidisciplinary care

sections.title: Choosing the First Test: Panel vs. Exome vs. Genome
sections.content:
The first test is a decision, not a default. Five branch points determine the right starting point. The [[diagnostic-yields|Diagnostic Yields]] module holds the full numbers; this section is the decision layer.

**1. How specific is the phenotype?** A tight, recognizable syndrome (e.g., classic Rett, tuberous sclerosis) points to **single-gene testing or a focused panel** — high pre-test probability. A broad or undifferentiated presentation (unexplained GDD/ID) points to **exome (or genome)**, which interrogates the whole coding space rather than betting on a short gene list.

**2. Are both parents available?** For severe, early-onset, de novo-enriched phenotypes (DEE, GDD with seizures, MCA), **trio** sequencing (proband + both parents) approximately doubles yield versus singleton — OR ~2.04 (Clark 2018) — and phases compound heterozygotes. When parents are available and the phenotype is severe and early-onset, default to trio.

**3. Does the picture suggest a repeat expansion?** Progressive ataxia, myotonic dystrophy, or a Huntington-like phenotype should trigger **dedicated repeat testing** (repeat-primed PCR, Southern blot, or long-read). Short-read WES/WGS does NOT reliably detect trinucleotide/pentanucleotide expansions.

**4. MCA/dysmorphism or infantile spasms?** CMA retains first-tier value: ~15–25% in multiple congenital anomalies, and 14% in infantile epileptic spasms (IESS) (vs. WES 26%). See [[cnv-interpretation|CNV Interpretation]] for what CMA detects (CNVs, aneuploidy, UPD/AOH on SNP arrays) and misses (SNVs, balanced rearrangements, repeat expansions).

**5. How urgent is turnaround?** An acutely ill NICU neonate needs **rapid WGS/WES** (35–50% yield; Maron JAMA 2023) — speed is the point, because diagnosis changes management in 38–50% of cases.

| Clinical situation | First test | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Recognizable tight syndrome | Single-gene / focused panel | High pre-test probability; fast, cheap |
| Undifferentiated GDD/ID, parents available | Trio exome (± concurrent CNV-seq) | ~2× yield (OR ~2.04, Clark 2018); de novo detection |
| Progressive ataxia / DM / HD-like | Dedicated repeat testing | Short-read WES/WGS misses expansions |
| MCA / dysmorphism | CMA first-tier | ~15–25% yield; detects CNVs/aneuploidy/UPD |
| Infantile epileptic spasms (IESS) | CMA + WES | CMA 14%, WES 26% (diagnostic-yields) |
| Acutely ill NICU neonate | Rapid WGS/WES | 35–50%; management changes 38–50% (Maron 2023) |

**Bottom line:** for most undifferentiated NDD/epilepsy with parents available, modern first-tier is **trio exome (± concurrent CNV-seq)**; CMA stays first-tier for MCA/dysmorphism; targeted panels fit phenotypically tight presentations; repeat disorders and NICU urgency each demand their own pathway.
keyPoints: Branch on phenotype specificity: tight recognizable syndrome -> single-gene/focused panel; broad/undifferentiated NDD -> exome (or genome)
For severe early-onset de novo-enriched phenotypes (DEE/GDD/MCA) with parents available, default to trio — ~doubles yield, OR ~2.04 (Clark 2018)
Repeat-expansion suspicion (progressive ataxia, DM1, Huntington) needs dedicated repeat testing; short-read WES/WGS does not reliably detect expansions
CMA stays first-tier for MCA/dysmorphism (~15–25%) and IESS (CMA 14% vs. WES 26%, diagnostic-yields)
Acutely ill NICU neonate -> rapid WGS/WES (35–50%; management changes in 38–50%, Maron JAMA 2023)

sections.title: Reading the Report: Living with a VUS
sections.content:
A **Variant of Uncertain Significance (VUS)** is exactly that: a variant for which the available evidence is insufficient to call it pathogenic or benign. It is NOT a partial diagnosis, a 'weak positive,' or a hedge — it is the honest statement that we do not yet know. How the lab arrives at this tier (the ACMG/AMP evidence codes) is covered in [[variant-interpretation|Variant Interpretation]]; this section is about what you do with one in the room.

**The cardinal rule: clinical decisions are not made on a VUS.** Under the ACMG/AMP 2015 standards (Richards et al. 2015), a VUS must not be used to confirm or exclude a diagnosis. Do not change management, initiate surveillance, alter treatment, or drive reproductive decisions on an unresolved VUS. Manage the patient on their clinical findings — as if the VUS had not been reported.

**Reclassification skews benign.** When VUS are later reclassified, the majority move toward benign rather than pathogenic. A VUS is therefore not 'probably the answer,' and presenting it as the likely cause manufactures false certainty that can harm the family.

**What to say vs. what not to say:**

| Say this | Not this |
|---|---|
| "We found a genetic spelling variation we can't yet interpret." | "We found a mutation." |
| "It does not confirm a diagnosis, and it does not rule one out." | "We found the cause." |
| "We'll manage your child on their symptoms, not on this result." | "We should start treatment for this." |
| "Our understanding may change as evidence grows." | "It's nothing / it's definitely the problem." |

**What can move a VUS over time:** periodic lab reclassification as databases grow; segregation and parental (trio) testing — confirming de novo status is often the single highest-yield step; deeper phenotyping; and functional or RNA studies. Set honest expectations about re-contact: responsibility for notifying you of a reclassification — lab versus ordering clinician — is **not standardized**. Do not promise the family an automatic system will reach them. Document the VUS with explicit uncertainty language and own the plan to revisit it (commonly reanalysis in 1–2 years).
keyPoints: A VUS means the evidence is insufficient to call pathogenic or benign — it is genuinely uncertain, not a partial or 'weak' diagnosis
Cardinal rule (ACMG/AMP 2015, Richards et al.): never base management, surveillance, treatment, or reproductive decisions on an unresolved VUS — manage on clinical findings
When VUS are reclassified, most move toward benign, not pathogenic — so a VUS should not be treated as 'probably the answer'
Framing matters: say 'a genetic spelling variation we can't yet interpret; it doesn't confirm a diagnosis' — never 'we found a mutation / we found the cause'

Parental/segregation testing, deeper phenotyping, functional/RNA studies, and periodic lab reclassification can move a VUS — but re-contact responsibility (lab vs. clinician) is not standardized, so document the VUS and own the plan to reanalyze

sections.title: When "Negative" Isn't Negative
sections.content:
A negative report is **time-stamped, not permanent**. It means no diagnostic variant was found *with today's knowledge, on this platform, in this tissue* — not that a genetic cause is excluded. Before declaring the workup done, run the phenotype past four under-the-radar blind spots, each with its own fix — see [[diagnostic-yields|Diagnostic Yields]] for the reanalysis and platform-yield numbers.

| What was missed | Why standard testing missed it | The fix |
|---|---|---|
| Real diagnosis, immature database | Gene-disease knowledge at the time of the original report didn't yet explain the variant | **Reanalysis** of existing exome data at 12–24 months — new diagnoses in ~10–25% of previously unsolved cases. The raw data didn't change; the interpretation framework did |
| Repeat expansion | Short-read WES/WGS does NOT reliably size trinucleotide/pentanucleotide expansions | **Dedicated repeat testing** — repeat-primed PCR, Southern blot, or long-read sequencing |
| Methylation / imprinting disorder | Not visible in sequence data alone — the defect is parent-of-origin methylation or UPD, not a coding variant | **Methylation-specific testing** (e.g., MS-MLPA at SNRPN) + **SNP-array CMA** for UPD |
| Mosaicism / wrong tissue | Somatic variant absent or very low-level in blood | **Deep-coverage sequencing** and/or sequencing of **affected tissue** (skin/biopsy) |

**The repeat-expansion blind spot — know the list.** Standard short-read sequencing misses: Friedreich ataxia (FXN GAA), spinocerebellar ataxias (CAG), CANVAS (RFC1 AAGGG), FXTAS (FMR1 CGG premutation), myotonic dystrophy DM1/DM2, Huntington disease (HTT CAG), and C9orf72 (ALS/FTD). A progressive ataxia, a myotonic or Huntington-like picture, or unexplained adult-onset tremor/ataxia should send you to dedicated repeat testing regardless of a 'negative' exome.

**Methylation and imprinting.** Angelman and Prader-Willi syndromes — and other imprinting disorders — are driven by methylation defects or UPD that sequence reads alone cannot see. The SNRPN methylation test detects ~99% of PWS and ~80% of AS; a normal result in a classic Angelman picture still prompts UBE3A sequencing — the [[epigenetics|Methylation & Imprinting]] module covers the parent-of-origin mechanics in detail.

**Mosaicism and tissue choice.** Somatic mosaic overgrowth (e.g., PIK3CA, AKT3) and brain-restricted variants causing focal cortical dysplasia or hemimegalencephaly may be absent from blood entirely. The route is deep-coverage sequencing of the affected tissue — skin, biopsy, or resected cortex — not a repeat of the blood test, as the [[mosaicism|Somatic Mosaicism]] module details.

**Below the detection floor.** Deep-intronic, regulatory, and structural variants below standard WES detection are next-step territory for genome sequencing or RNA-seq.

**The clinical reflex:** after every negative result, ask *which of these blind spots fits this phenotype?* before calling the workup complete.
keyPoints: A negative report is time-stamped, not permanent: it reflects today's knowledge, this platform, and this tissue — not exclusion of a genetic cause
Database immaturity: reanalysis of existing exome data at 12–24 mo yields new diagnoses in ~10–25% of previously unsolved cases (diagnostic-yields) — same raw data, updated interpretation

Repeat-expansion blind spot: short-read WES/WGS misses Friedreich (FXN GAA), SCA (CAG), CANVAS (RFC1 AAGGG), FXTAS (FMR1 CGG premutation), DM1/DM2, Huntington (HTT CAG), C9orf72 — fix with repeat-primed PCR, Southern blot, or long-read

Imprinting disorders (Angelman, Prader-Willi) need methylation-specific testing (MS-MLPA) + SNP-array CMA for UPD — invisible to sequence alone; somatic overgrowth (PIK3CA, AKT3) needs deep-coverage or affected-tissue sequencing (blood may miss it)

Clinical reflex: after a negative result, ask 'which blind spot fits this phenotype?' — and consider genome sequencing or RNA-seq for deep-intronic/regulatory/structural variants below standard WES detection

sections.title: After the Diagnosis: Treatment & Surveillance
sections.content:
A molecular diagnosis is not the end of the workup — it reframes management.

**Disease-modifying vs. symptomatic.** A **disease-modifying** therapy alters the underlying biology or natural history; **symptomatic/supportive** care treats the manifestations without changing the course. For a growing list of monogenic conditions, a precise molecular diagnosis is the gateway to disease-modifying treatment — see [[therapies|Therapies]] and [[neuromuscular|Neuromuscular Disease]]. In SMA, SMN-restoring therapy (nusinersen, an intrathecal ASO; risdiplam, an oral SMN2 splicing modifier; onasemnogene abeparvovec, AAV9-SMN1 gene replacement) transforms the natural history and is most effective given presymptomatically. In DMD, exon-skipping ASOs (e.g., eteplirsen for exon-51-amenable deletions) restore the reading frame in eligible genotypes. None of these can be offered without the exact molecular result.

**Precision symptomatic / metabolic treatment.** Even when no disease-modifying drug exists, the genotype often dictates the right symptomatic choice — and the wrong one to avoid (see [[epilepsy|Epilepsy]] and [[iem|Inborn Errors of Metabolism]]). GLUT1 deficiency (SLC2A1) responds to the **ketogenic diet**; pyridoxine-dependent epilepsy (ALDH7A1) responds to **pyridoxine (B6)**. The genotype also flags drugs to *avoid*: in SCN1A/Dravet, **avoid sodium-channel blockers** (oxcarbazepine, lamotrigine), which worsen seizures; in SLC6A1, **valproate is first-line** (do not confuse with SCN1A); in ALDH5A1/SSADH, **avoid vigabatrin** (paradoxical GABA elevation). The molecular diagnosis thus unlocks targeted therapy, flags contraindicated drugs, and ends the diagnostic odyssey.

**Surveillance: the diagnosis triggers a program.** A confirmed genetic diagnosis activates a defined surveillance schedule for known complications — a core reason genetic diagnosis changes management. Tuberous sclerosis complex (TSC) is the model, with clear international consensus (the 2021 International TSC Surveillance and Management recommendations, Northrup et al. 2021); see [[neurodevelopmental-disorders|Neurodevelopmental Disorders]] for TSC clinical detail.

| Organ system | What to monitor | Interval (Northrup 2021) |
|---|---|---|
| Brain | SEGA (subependymal giant cell astrocytoma) | MRI every 1–3 yr if asymptomatic and < 25 yr |
| Kidney | Angiomyolipoma, renal cysts | MRI every 1–3 yr, lifelong |
| Neurodevelopment | TAND (TSC-associated neuropsychiatric disorders) | Annual screen; full evaluation at key developmental ages |
| Heart | Cardiac rhabdomyoma | Echocardiogram every 1–3 yr in asymptomatic children until regression; ECG every 3–5 yr, all ages |
| Eyes | Retinal lesions; vigabatrin visual-field toxicity | Annual ophthalmologic exam |
| Skin / teeth | Skin lesions; dental review | Annual skin exam; dental review at least every 6 months |

**Bottom line:** after a diagnosis, ask three questions — is there a disease-modifying therapy, does the genotype change symptomatic drug choices (including drugs to avoid), and what surveillance does this diagnosis now mandate?
keyPoints: Disease-modifying therapy alters the disease course; symptomatic care treats manifestations — and a precise molecular diagnosis is the gateway to disease-modifying options (matches therapies module)

SMA is disease-modifiable by SMN restoration — nusinersen (intrathecal ASO), risdiplam (oral SMN2 splicing modifier), onasemnogene abeparvovec (AAV9-SMN1); DMD by exon-skipping ASOs such as eteplirsen for exon-51-amenable deletions (matches therapies + neuromuscular modules)
Genotype-directed symptomatic treatment: ketogenic diet for GLUT1 deficiency (SLC2A1); pyridoxine (B6) for pyridoxine-dependent epilepsy (ALDH7A1) (matches epilepsy + iem modules)

Genotype flags drugs to avoid: avoid sodium-channel blockers (oxcarbazepine, lamotrigine) in SCN1A/Dravet; valproate is first-line in SLC6A1 (not to be confused with SCN1A); avoid vigabatrin in ALDH5A1/SSADH (matches epilepsy module exactly)

A confirmed genetic diagnosis triggers a defined surveillance program for known complications — e.g., TSC has international consensus (Northrup et al. 2021): brain MRI every 1–3 yr if asymptomatic and < 25 yr, renal MRI every 1–3 yr lifelong, annual TAND screening, echocardiogram every 1–3 yr in asymptomatic children until rhabdomyoma regression, ECG every 3–5 yr

After a diagnosis, ask three questions: is there a disease-modifying therapy, does the genotype change symptomatic drug choices (including drugs to avoid), and what surveillance does this diagnosis now mandate?
